Hon. SYDNEY FISHER (Minister of Agriculture) moved for leave to introduce (Bill No. 151) respecting the Incorporation of Seed-Growers' Association.
What is the purpose of the Bill?

It is simply to give statutory authority for the incorporation of Seed-Growers' Associations. In consequence of the investigations that have been made by my department into the seed business of the country, certain people have expressed a wish to form themselves into an association for growing seed grain and other agricultural seeds. At present, there is no law under which these people can be incorporated and do their work legally as a corporate body. Some years ago parliament passed a statute for the incorporation of live stock associations, and this Bill is very much in the same form, as applied to seed growers.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

House again went into committee on Bill (No. 5) respecting the Militia of Canada-Sir Frederick Borden.

speakeroldname: Hon. SIR FREDERICK BORDEN (Minister of Militia).
speechtext:
When the second reading of this Bill was under discussion, my hon. friend from South Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale) who preceded me in the department of Militia, asked for some papers with reference to the communications which led up to my attendance at the meeting of the Defence Committee in London. I told the hon. gentleman that I would endeavour to bring these papers down. I have them here. They consist of only two or three cablegrams which I will read. The first was from Mr. Chamberlain to Lord Minto :-
London, April 20, 1903.
With regard to important amendment contemplated in Militia Act, His Majesty's government earnestly hopes that your responsible advisers will defer action until matter has been fully discussed by Minister of Militia with Secretary of State for War and Commander in Chief. After close of Dominion session of parliament would suggest that Sir Frederick Borden should come to England.
(Sgd.) CHAMBERLAIN.
Ottawa, Nov. 12, 1903.
Referring to Mr. Chamberlain's cypher telegram dated 20th April, Minister of Militia 203
anxious to sail for England about Nov. 28th, so that he may discuss new Militia Act with Secretary of State for War and Commander in Chief, and return to Canada before Christmas. Hope that this arrangement may be a convenient one. Consider mutual discussion important.
(Sgd.) MINTO.
Lord Minto telegraphed later on
Ottawa, 23rd Nov., 1903.
Am anxious for reply to my telegram of Nov. 12th, as Minister of Militia wishes to make his plans accordingly.
(Sgd.) MINTO.
The answer from Mr. Littleton was as follows
London, 24th Nov., 1903.
Referring to your cable of yesterday's date. Date suggested for visit of minister will be quite convenient.
(Sgd.) LYTTLETON.
I have already stated to the House the substance of what took place at that meeting of the Defence Committee. I only wish to add that my understanding of the object of my being invited to attend that meeting was simply and solely to expedite business. The Defence Committee is no longer, as it used to be, a sub-committee of Council, but is now an independent and advisory committee which has been created by the Prime Minister of England for the purpose of advising the Council, and its functions go no further than those of advisers. It is a business committee, and the object of inviting me to attend that committee, was simply7 to bring about, in the shortest possible manner the best results. As a result of my attending that committee, we were able to arrange in a short time-in an hour and a half or so-business that could not have been done in less than weeks, or possibly months, by correspondence.
Since the conymittee last sat, a number of notices of proposed amendments have been given. I have collected all of these amendments, with the exception of one or two, for the convenience of hon. gentlemen who are interested in this discussion, and I shall send two copies of this memorandum to bon. gentlemen opposite. The further amendments will be explained later on. Since the Bill was prepared I have, as already indicated to the House, had an opportunity of studying the new system which has been adopted by the War Office, as the result of ihe report of the committee known as the Esher Committee, which was appointed by Mr. Balfour for the purpose of investigating and reporting on all matters connected with the organization of the War Office, and making a report. The report is known as the Report of the War Office (Reconstitution) Committee, and is an exceedingly interesting, able and elaborate document. This report lias been adopted by the British government, and the details of it are now being worked cut. Like any new system it will, of course.



take time to work out all the details, but the main principles have been adopted and, I have been informed, are working very well. In view of the course which has been pursued by the War Office, a course which I may say has resulted from difficulties which were found to exist in working out the complicated system which has obtained in England, and which, to some extent, has been in existence in this country, I have thought it advisable to provide, in the Bill now before parliament, the machinery by which the government of this country may follow the example of the Imperial Government. Without troubling this committee by going into details, I think I may say, without fear of contradiction, that it is quite obvious that the system which has been in existence in this country ever since confederation has not worked well. I am not going to animadvert upon or criticise any officers who have been sent out here to assist us in administering the militia of this country. I do not propose to do that, but 1 think that every one will agree that the system has not worked well, and I am prepared to blame the system much more than the individuals who have attempted to work it. I believe it is an impossible system. I believe it is absolutely and entirely impossible to get on with the system which we have attempted to work in this country since confederation. We have had abundant examples, not confined to the administrations of the Liberal party alone, but under previous administrations as well, when It was found unworkable. There are many difficulties which I think act against the public interest in the endeavour to work out this system, difficulties which will be overcome entirely or very largely by the new system. One of these difficulties is that there has been absolute want of continuity under the existing system. Each new General Officer Commanding who comes to this country seems to be possessed with the idea that it is his duty to overturn and change everything done by his predecessor. There are no records to show in detail the reasons for the conclusions which the different General Officers Commanding have reached. Lnder the new system, there will be a Militia Council corresponding to what is in England called the Army Council. That council will be composed of the Minister of Militia, as chairman of the council, with four military men and two additional civilians. Everything that is done at that council will be made a matter of record, or at any rate every conclusion of importance which is reached by that council will be made a matter of record, so that if there be a change of ministers or a change of officers the record will remain there for the guidance of those who may come afterwards, and when changes are suggested, means will be found to compare new proposals with old proposals.
Are those means not available now ?
I am not aware of that being the ease ; they were not found available in the British War Office, and they are very much less likely to be available here.
You are describing the British system now ?

Yes. That is the system which I propose to inaugurate in this country. Of course, the conditions being changed, it was necessary to change some of the provisions with reference to the formation and working out of the system. The Militia Council, as I say, will be composed of seven members, as is the Army Council-four military, three civil. The Minister for the time being will be the chairman ; the principal military officer will be known as the Chief of the General Staff. Then there will be the Adjutant General, the Quartermaster-General and the Master-General of Ordnance. The two additional civilians would be the Deputy Minister and, probably, the Chief Accountant of the Department.
Why not have the Finance Minister of Canada ?
My hon. friend will have an opportunity of criticising these proposals later on.
Or the Auditor General ?

That might add to the harmony of things. The minister in this way will have the advantage of being surrounded by his officers, by all the leading men representing the leading departments of the militia service. He will be in constant touch with his officers, and will, for the first time, have an opportunity of knowing exactly what is going on. He will have an opportunity of hearing and exchanging opinions with the technical men. which-if he happens to be an inexperienced man when he comes into office, as he is very likely to be-will be a very great advantage to him.
As I understand this advisory council, it is to consist of men in the service of the department.
Yes.
Are you not iu the position to call on them now ? Would it not be better to have men from the outside ?

I am discussing a change which involves dispensing altogether with the services of
the General Officer Commanding, and the council will be largely in substitution of that office. With reference to the question
63(59

which my hon. friend has Just put, I might answer it by pointing to the experience which I have had, and the correspondence in connection with which I read to this House three or four years ago, over a controversy with the General Officer Commanding. I was under the impression that I had the right to consult any officer in my department, and I was doing so when I discovered that an order had been sent out by the General Officer Commanding to each one of these gentlemen not to come to my office without his permission, and after they had come with his permission and discussed matters with me. they were immediately to go back to him and tell him every word that had taken place.
Would the minister kindly name the general ?
I think my hon. friend knows who it was. It was General Hutton.

You have
heard of him.

1 may say in addition that I blame the system. These men come here with the idea that they are to command, and that every officer in the Dominion is absolutely under them and them alone, and they are jealous of any interference even by the minister. They) object apparently to the minister, who is responsible to parliament and the people, having any direct communication with the officers under him. That is one of the difficulties of the system. It is a difficulty which was found to prevail in England and rendered the system there unworkable. The same difficulty exists here to a very much greater degree. I do not know that I need go further into the Bill just now, because I think the better way Is to discuss the section as it comes up. In the discussion we bad, many suggestions of importance were made, and I have endeavoured in the new sections to meet these as far as possible. When I introduced the Bill I said we would drop the word ' Defence,' from the old title of ' Militia and Defence.' I have ascertained from the officers of my department that this change is undesirable, because it would render useless large quantities of forms.
Would not there eventually be a saving in the amount of printing by the omission of this useless word ?
We have a great many forms printed now. I move, therefore, that the title of the Bill be made to read ' An Act respecting the Department of Militia and Defence.'
Does that mean that we have given up the idea of a navy V
No.

Or has it been handed over to the Minister of Agriculture V 2031
The hon. minister has just told us that these men come over here with the idea that they are to command, and objects to the minister interfering with the officers under him. Will he give some instances to illustrate that other than General Hutton ?
I am afraid my hon. friend will have to take my statement, which is the result of my experience.

I think that these gentlemen's reputations are of as much value to them as the minister's is to him. if they have been unfair or unreasonable, we should know, but it is hardly fair to General O'Grady-Haly or Lord Dundonald or any of the others, that a general reflection such as this should be made which might apply to any one of them.

What I said was that I blamed the system and not the individual, and when I mentioned General Hutton in reply to the question put by my hon. friend, I had no intention of being drawn into any personal controversy with reference to any of these General Officers Commanding. I knew that the hon. member for Victoria does not object in the slightest degree to any unpleasant or unfavourable remarks regarding General Hutton, and as the matter affecting that general had come before the House, and was on record, I referred to the correspondence. I have said that the system is unworkable, but that implies no reflection on the officers themselves. They were sent out, as they supposed, to command. Every officer in Canada is under them, every officer of the Headquarters Staff is under them, but under the new system there will be no question of rank affecting this Military Council. That is carefully left out. The men who come in will come in on an equal footing and,their position will be altogether different from that of the General Officer Commanding.

The hon. minister has made a statement in regard to myself that I cannot allow to pass. He said	that he	knew that his hon.
friend, meaning myself, would take no objection to anything unpleasant which he might say regarding General Hutton. I have been fair to General Hutton throughout the length and breadth of the British empire, and what I would object to in General Hutton I would object to in Lord Dundonald. I do object to any commanding officer coming to this country and seeking to arrogate to himself functions that belong to the people of Canada, but we must be just as careful that the minister in charge of the department' does not arrogate to himself functions that do not belong to him. I have been absolutely fair to General Hutton, and I do not think the ,hon. minister has any right to make the statement that I have been unfair to him.

What I say is that this is part of the system. The system is to blame. I do not blame any one in particular, but under the system, as it now exists, the commanding officer commands every officer in Canada and nobody knows better than my hon. friend what that means in the matter of discipline. It is a very difficult position to place an officer in to expect him to be entirely satisfied that officers acting in a subordinate capacity under him shall come to the minister as often as they choose, or as often as he may wish to see them, to consult about matters about which he thinks they ought to be consulted. I am not finding any fault. I am sorry if I have been unable to make myself understood. I am not blaming any officer in particular ; I am blaming the system and it is the system we propose to change.
W'ould the hon. minister kindly state again the officers who are to form a council ?
I will mention them when we get to that clause.

The hon. minister tells us that he proposes to change the system and adopt that which is recommended in England. Would not the conditions in connection with the militia of England be so Mr. SAM. HUGHES.
different from what they are in Canada that we could hardly apply the same system ?

No doubt the conditions would be different, but not so very different. I am not speaking without the book. I have taken the pains to consult some of the most eminent military authorities in England as well as in this country, and they agree that while there may be some difficulties and that while some alterations may have to be made in applying the system, it can be applied here equally as well as in England.

In having read the document the hon. gentleman has referred to, it is a very extensive document and it refers particularly to the system in England. It occurred to me at the time I read it that the conditions were so very different here from those which exist in England as to make it difficult to apply the same system.

I think that so far as the reconstitution of the Headquarters Staff is concerned the conditions are similar to those of the War Office in England, and I cannot see any difficulty at all on that score. All my hon. friends who have written me on the subject and some of the most eminent military authorities agree that there will be no difficulty whatever in applying the system so far as the W nr Office is concerned. When it comes to the question of decentralization it may be that we shall not be able to go as far in this country as they have gone in England. I do not think that policy can be carried out in connection with the militia force as easily as in connection with the regular army.

Under the proposed amendment of the Militia Act which has been brought down by the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence, it is optional whether we have a commanding officer from England or not. I judge from the tone of the hon. gentleman's language to-day that it is not intended to have a Major General from England in the future. Coupling the change in the system which it is proposed to adopt with the language the hon. gentleman has used are we correct in assuming that we are not in the future to have a General Officer Commanding ?

Under the system there will be no General Officer Commanding. There is no Commander in Chief in England to-day and there will be no General Officer Commanding here. There would be a first military officer known as the Chief of the General Staff, the most important military officer in the country as he is to-day the most important military officer in England, except some of the generals commanding in chief in some of the large districts. Under the new system we would have more

important commands than we have to-day. Decentralization would be carried out to some extent, perhaps not to the same extent as in England, so that officers commanding districts would have much greater powers than they have at the present moment, and properly so, because these men, if they are ever to be fit to comamnd, must have experience in times of peace which will enable them to perform the duties which may (be required of them in times of war.

Is not that one of the very reasons why we require an experienced man in this country The officers of Canada have not had experience in handling large bodies of men, and for that reason it seems to me that we should have an English officer of experience in this country. You will have four or five of these officers and if so are there in that number any who are capable of handling large bodies of men ?

I believe there are. I believe, however, that if we never make the attempt we never will learn. Our officers must have experience. I believe they can learn if given an opportunity. They have not been given an opportunity. We think that under this system we shall be able to develop our men. especially as we have been able to make an arrangement with the War Office by which two places are to be given each year to Canadian officers to enable them to learn their duties in the Staff College in England. We shall, after this. I hope, always have two of our men at the Staff College in England learning the staff duties.
On section 2, paragraph (f),
' General Orders ' means orders and instructions issued to the militia by the General Officer Commanding, with the approval of the Minister of Militia.
I move to strike out the words ' by the General Officer Commanding.' >
Does that mean that the minister will issue orders ?
They will be issued by the Council.

This clause gives power to the minister to issue orders. Suppose the Minister of Agriculture was acting Minister of Militia again ; he got the country into one mess already, and under this he could issue any orders lie likes; perhaps to take the heads of these officers down to Sweets-burg.
My hon. friend is facetious.

It is bad enough to have the Minister of Militia given this authority without military advice, but suppose we have another episode similar to
the little conspiracy we exposed the other day where will we land ?
As a matter of fact the Minister of Militia must approve. "

But suppose the minister choses to act without the consent of his Council he has power under this clause, and we will have a little dictatorship.
I admit the minister must endorse the views of the Council but the Council has not the power to interfere with the views of the minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We will let that paragraph stand.
Under section 123, the Governor in Council makes the regulations.
I do not quite understand the effect of the word ' emergency ' here. In view of the powers given the government under section 77 ; powers by the way which I very strongly object to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Who do you object to ?
I object to the word ' emergency ' here because of the wide powers given the government in section 77 where the Governor in Council has power to send the militia out of Canada.
Rut only for the defence of Canada.

You can call almost anything the defence of Canada-you could call sending the militia to any part of the British empire doing it for the defence of Canada. The Governor General in Council should not have power to do that ; that power should remain in the hands of parliament alone.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have had that power for a long time.

That makes no difference, we are now discussing this Bill which makes changes in many directions and the existing law can be changed as well in this respect. I do not believe in this centralization of power in the Governor in Council. It would seem that every Act passed in this parliament now inclines to give more power to the government of the day. Parliament has no rigiit to divest itself of its inherent powers; we are here as the representatives of the people and we should hold this power in our own hands. Whether for the defence of Canada or not, the militia of Canada should not he sent out of Canada without the authority of parliament. There can be no 'emergency' arise under which parliament cannot be called together ; war does not spring up in a day or a night. ' If the country were in danger of war it would be an easy matter to call parliament and then parliament could decide if it is necessary to

6376'
send our militia outside of Canada. It is a different matter altogether about permitting volunteers to serve in any portion of the empire.

Under the law in Great Britain, parliament must be called within a certain time after the militia are embodied; ten days I think. Why not insert a similar provision in this Bill. I think the Governor in Council should have authority to call out the militia, but parliament should be assembled within a reasonable time afterwards. I do not want to be too captious with my hon, friend (Mr. Fowler) with whom I agree in almost everything, but I cannot endorse him when he speaks about ' permitting ' Canadians to serve the empire as volunteers.
I maintain that no man requires any permission from any authority in the Dominion of Canada to volunteer to serve the empire in any part of the world. He requires no commission, direct or indirect, from the Governor, the Prime Minister, the Govenor in Council or the parliament of Canada, and the imperial authorities have an absolute right to put their recruiting sergeant in the city of Ottawa to-day, and recruit men without let or hindrance of any authority in Canada, to serve the empire in any part of the world.

I would like to point out to the hon. member for King's N.B. (Mr. Fowler) that the law now in existence gives wider power than the section of this Bill to which he takes exception. Under the present law,
His Majesty may call out the militia or any part thereof for active service, either within or without Canada, at any time when it appears advisable to do so, by reason of war, invasion or insurrection, or danger of any of them.
Under the proposed law :
The Governor in Council may place the militia, or any part thereof, on active service anywhere in Canada and also beyond Canada for the defence thereof.
This is a decided limitation as compared with the existing law. While I agree with my hon. friend that matters of such importance should be at once submitted to parliament, and parliament should be called, and would be called, nevertheless an emergency might occur when it would be absolutely necessary on the frontier to take advantage of military tactics for the complete defence of Canada. The matter might have to be decided in an hour or a minute.
Mr.SAM. HUGHES. Does not the minister think it would be well to have a clause inserted in this Act similar to that in the English law, providing that parliament should be called say within ten days ?
That might be, but my hon. friend will see that while in England there is a standing army of 200,000
or 300,000 men, our militia is the only defence we have.
We have a standing army just as large proportionately.
Oh, no.

What the minister says in regard to the present law is a matter of common knowledge. But we are changing that, and how is the time to make the thing right. The power should be entirely in the hands of parliament. According to. this Act, even if parliament were sitting, the Governor in Council has power to legislate without consulting parliament at all. It seems to me that that is wrong.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
At the present moment we are simply defining what is an emergency, and I do not think my hon. friend will take exception to the definition. By section 77, to which my hon. friend has alluded, the Governor in Council is given certain powers in case of emergency. Perhaps those powers are too great or are not great enough. That is a question to be discussed when we reach section 77 ; but it seems to me that no exception can be taken by my hon. friend to the definition of emergency, which is the only thing before us at present.
.[DOT] Mr. R. L. BORDEN. I do not quite understand subsection (f) and there is some information which I shall require when we come to consider it again. When I mentioned my objection, I was referred to section 123, which deals, not with general orders, but with regulations ; and they seem to be two distinct things. Section 123 is relevant to subsection (h) but not to subsection (f). When we come to discuss (f) again, I would like a more definite answer to the question I asked a moment ago.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I asked that (f) be allowed to stand, for this reason, because it is understood, according to the views of my hon. friend, that we are to dispense with five services of the General Officer Commanding. The duties now performed by him are to be largely performed by an advisory commission. At present, a' general order means an order issued to the militia by the General Officer Commanding, with the approval of the Minister of Militia. That is to say, there are two authorities, the commanding officer and the minister.
I presume it is the intention of the minister to substitute somebody for the General Officer Commanding, because the regula-lations ought to be approved by somebody else before they are sanctioned by the minister himself. That is the reason I asked that this clause stand.

They should be
made by somebody and approved by the minister. I would like some further information as to just what the minister means
(by the proposed change of system. I undlar-stood him to say that under the present sys-

tem the minister does not communicate with the subordinate officers directly; but some change is to be made in that regard. Is it to be a general change ? As I understand the present system, if the General Officer wants to communicate orders to the battalion or to subordinate officers, he does so through some person who is near in command to himself.
Through the adjutant-general.
And the adjutant-general communicates with the district officer commanding, who in turn communicates with the commanding officer of the regiment. Is that the system which it is intended to change ?

No, that system will not be changed ; but instead of the General Officer Commanding, the proposed Militia Board will fix the policy, issue orders, and deal with all questions connected with the administration of the militia.

I understood that there were to be some omissions in the means by which the orders were to be communicated. Is it meant that the proposed council is to communicate, for example, directly with the commanding officer of a regiment ? I am not very clear as to what the change is, and I would like to understand it.

I think the hon. leader of the opposition does not understand the situation referred to by the Minister of Militia. He did not refer to conditions such as those which have recently been before us, in which the Minister of Agriculture arrogated to himself, either of his own right or as acting Minister of Militia, to meddle with the formation of a regiment. I think the minister himself, if allowed to speak the truth would condemn that. But what the minister referred to was what, according to rumour, happened when General Hutton was here. The minister chose to speak to one of his departmental officers, but General Hutton refused to allow the officer to approach the minister except through him. I think the minister was justified in the course he took; but I think it is also courteous for him to notify the General Officer Commanding of any action he takes. I do not think the hon. leader of the opposition understood that.

I think I understood it, but I want to know what the system is to be-whether you are to keep up the old form of giving out instructions through a series of officers, or whether you are to have a different system ?
The Minister of Militia will keep the same relative control that he does at this moment.
Well, what change is to be made with regard to communicating instructions ?

The chief of the General Staff, who is the new officer, will have charge of what are called field operations-charge of preparing an army for the field. The Adjutant-General will have charge of certain branches, many of them the same as now-education, mobilization, &c. The Quartermaster-General will have charge of very much the same things as now-transportation and so on. And the Master-General of Ordnance will have charge of the ordnance, guns and.so on. Each one of these men will be supreme in his own department, subject of course to the decisions of the Militia Council, and these are the men who would compose the Militia Council.

HUGHEiS. The hon. minister does not understand what the leader of the opposition wants to know. Under the new system will it be possible for the Minister of Militia or the Minister of Agriculture, as acting in his place, to have officers appointed, the recommendations of whom does not come through the regular channel ? Will it be possible for the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Militia to interfere directly in the appointment of officers ?

As regards appointments, under the new system there will be a new method. According to the English- system, which I am very much inclined to approve of, that work is all done absolutely independent of headquarters, except that finally, I suppose, the Minister of Militia will have to approve. We cannot very well get around that. This Bill cannot go into force until proper regulations are carefully made, and I could not say at the moment what system will be adopted, but in a general way, greater powers will be given the districts than they have now.
Who is to be the recognized General Officer Commanding 1
The Militia Council.
In that case the order passed in October last applying to General Officers Commanding will be entirely wiped out ?
Certainly.
Who will sign these appointments ?
The Militia Council will act very largely in the sphere within which the Commander in Chief now acts in England. The signing of the appointments is a matter of detail.

I think it is a matter of very great importance. If the chief staff officer is a man of any military quali-

fication, he should assume responsibility from the military point of view.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As a non-combatant, may I offer a suggestion. We have to determine what will be the character of the body which is to replace the General Officer Commanding. Would it not be well to allow this matter to remain in abeyance until we have threshed out that question and determined what will take the place of the General Officer or what body will assume his duties.

That body will be civil as well as military, but there should be a special committee to deal with til? question of recommendations for commissions on the force from a purely military standpoint, as it is now dealt with by the General Officer Commanding.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would it not be wiser to discuss all that when we are discussing the organization of the body ?

I am bringing it up now so that the minister may have it in his mind.
All the paragraphs agreed to accept paragraph (f.)
On section 4,
The commander in chief of the militia is vested in the King, and shall be exercised and administered by His Majesty or by the Governor General as his representative
In what does this differ from the old clause ?
The word 1 personally ' is left out.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would suggest that this whole section would be dropped. It is absolutely unnecessary and in any event would have to be altered. Section 15 of the British North America Act provides :
The command in chief of the land and naval militia, and of all naval and military forces, of and in Canada, is hereby declared to continue to be vested in the Queen.
That does away with the necessity for this section.
Let the section stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If it is to stand, I would suggest this modification. Instead of reading. ' The command in chief of thc-militia is vested in the King,' it should read, as in the words of the British North America Act, ' is hereby declared to continue and be vested in the King.' Because we are not conferring upon His Majesty authority over the army. That authority is conferred by the constitution.
I beg to make a suggestion to the minister. Clause 4 of the present Bill, which corresponds to clause

3 of the existing Act, declares that the command in chief of the militia belongs to the King, and as the Minister of Justice has properly said, we have no power to give any right or power to the King ; section 15 of the British North American Act defines the power of the King, so far as the militia is concerned. But clause 4 of this Bill defines not only the power of the King, but the power of the Governor General. Though the sovereign power, the sovereign command of the militia of any British colony, belongs as does tbe command of the army of England, to' the King, yet the exercise of the command, the organization of the army, belongs exclusively and solely to the parliament of England, as the organization of the militia in any of the self-governing colonies belongs exclusively and solely to the parliament of the colony. And, in the case of a selfgoverning colony, as in the case of England. parliament delegates such power as it pleases to the government. This section should not only be a declaration of tlie sovereign right of the King, which everybody agrees to, but it should declare clearly so that it may be understood that the Canadian parliament is as supreme in the governing of militia matters as in others, and therefore. I think it should contain a provision similar to the present clause of the cld Act, but clearer. I would suggest the wording :
The command in chief of the militia is hereby declared to continue and be vested in the King, and shall be administered and exercised by the Governor General in Council.
That will very clearly and properly define tbe power of the King and leave it untouched, but it will make equally clear that the exercise of the King's command of the militia belongs to the Governor General in Council according to the powers granted by this parliament under this Bill. In fact throughout this Bill in every clause where under the existing Act power is given to the King, or to His Majesty or to the Governor General, it is changed, and the words that appear are :	* Governor General in
Council.' In fact, in about twenty clauses of the Bill now before us the principle of self-government is asserted in this way. Therefore, it seems to me, in defining the powers which are to be exercised by those to whom the exercise of these powers is to be committed, it seems to me that the same form should be used so as to make it clear that the exercise of the sovereign power over the militia belongs to the Governor General in Council, under authority conferred by this parliament.

I am sure the hon. member (Mr. Bourassa) has thrown no new light upon the question. Every one knows that 1 Governor General ' means * Governor General in Council.' So far as the

control of the army In England Is concerned, the King has no authority direct or indirect. And the same is true of Canada. ' The King can do no wrong,' because the King acts upon the advice of his responsible ministers.

Of course, there is no dispute as to that. But if the Minister of Militia and the government think fit to replace the words ' His Majesty,' and ' Governor General ' with the words,
' Governor General in Council.' in other parts of the Bill, it seems to me only reasonable to make this section in harmony with the rest of the Bill not only in spirit but in wording. I admit that it is more a question of wording than a question of policy, but, at the same time, it seems quite proper that the wording should be clear and consistent. I admit that, if all classes of the people of the country, and all of parliament, were imbued with strong principles of nati >nnl self-government, there would be no necessity to put in these words. But as we have heard strange constitutional doctrine in this parliament as well as outside of it, doctrine that, if carried out, would limit or, ignore the self-governing powers of this country, this parliament, and this government in militia matters, I think it is only proper that the principle should be laid down clearly in the early clauses of the Bill as is done throughout the rest of it. What I ask is simply to put the clause now under consideration in harmony with the principles and the wording of the rest of the measure. There is nothing new in what I propose and I certainly am not suggesting anything revolutionary.

I differ from the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bourassa) who wants to drive a wedge-that is the meaning of it -between Canada and the mother country. Why is he not square and honest ? Everybody knows the constitutional principles that govern this country. Th? King is Commander in Chief here as in England, and here we exercise the prerogative as parliament exercises it in England. He has only to give us under our constitution the right to exercise that prerogative in this parliament the same as exercised in England. The King's prerogative in the government of the militia of this country devolves upon this parliament, and any attempt to carry that prerogative further than it is carried now would be an attempt to drive a wedge between the old country and this country- And I am surprised that the hon. gentleman on all these occasions should exhibit a disposition to tear this country away in every way by legislation from the old country. I do not wish to be offensive to any hon. gentleman in this House, and I will not; but I am bound to be honest and square ; and, in that spirit I say that I am sorry that the hon. member from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) always seems to me to exhibit a desire to establish something in this country hostile to the interests of Canada as a part of the empire. His attempt is simply to set up the prerogative in Canada in opposition to the prerogative of the King.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: I move that the words ' and Defence ' be added after ' Minister of Militia.'
Amendment agreed to.
How does this section correspond with the present section ?
It is practically the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It substitutes the w ord ' may ' for the word ' shall.' This is a mere improvement in the drafting.

I would not draw attention to this section but for the peculiar doctrine given to the Dominion of Canada by an Order in Council of this government which establishes as a precedent the right of any minister, in his own district, tc have official authority. Does not the Prime Minister agree that that is the meaning of the Order in Council ? The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), for instance, has the right to step in and override this in his own district ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes) states that the Order in Council lays down the doctrine that a minister has absolute authority in his own district. The Order in Council says nothing of that kind. It says-and I think it will not be questioned by the hon. gentleman himself-that every minister is supposed to look after the interests of his own section.
In all departments ?
Is this to apply in all senses ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In ail senses, Mr. INGRAM. Well, let us apply that and see where it will end. It is a recognized fact that every minister of the Crown is a political head, and he will naturally do that which he thinks will advance the interests of the political party to which he belongs. Hon. gentlemen opposite have always laid down the principle that there should not be any party politics in connection with military matters in this country. I want to knowT from the Minister of Militia or the Prime Minister how you are going to have military discipline that is to be purely nonpolitical. to have no partisan conduct or action in connection with the militia of this country, if you are going to allow any political head to have anything to do with the internal administration of the militia ? I can quite understand that rule applying in any minister's district where anything was involved that might fairly be viewed as a partisan matter or something to be done ir. the interest of the government from a partisan standpoint, but militia matters should be kept entirely aloof from considerations of this kind. Why ? Because if you want to have discipline in the militia of this country you must certainly not have any interference from the outside. If the minister wants to reorganize a militia battalion he will give his instructions through the proper channels and will receive his information from the usual channel and that channel is not a partisan channel. That is if the statement of the hon. gentleman is a correct statement, namely, that he is not administering) his department in the interest of party. Is it not a fact that even the corporal is jealous of his rights in the matter of discipline ? If you go over a corporal's head in order to give directions to his military inferiors, he at once becomes jealous. You are interfering with the discipline. If you go over the lieutenant to the captain you create a feeling of jealousy. The only way to administer the militia is to administer it through the proper channels. What would be the situation of a lieutenant-colonel of any battalion if he were to communicate direct to the minister instead of communicating through the usual military channel ? Imagine the Minister of Agriculture giving his instructions, imagine his interference in the matter of this kind. And then imagine any hon. gentleman saying that we have no partisanship in the affairs of the militia of this country. I say that it is simply impossible and what I fear to-day and fear in the future, the words :
General Officer Commanding ' being struck out. is that instead of having non-partisan feeling throughout the militia of this country as we have had for many years, we are opening the door wide for the introduction of partisan feeling into the administration of the militia. I regret very much indeed that the hon. minister's language has been changed Mr. INGRAM.
to-day from what it was at the introduction of this Bill. As it was at first, if Canada felt disposed to have an English officer as General Officer Commanding she could have one, and if a Canadian happened to be available for the position, a Canadian could be appointed. The minister has closed the door absolutely to-day against the employment of an English officer. By the argument he has used, this situation is brought about although the Bill does not say so. I. for one protest against the understanding conveyed by the Prime Minister to-day, that any minister of the Crown will have the right to interfere with the appointments made in our militia. I, for one, am a strong believer . in the principle that the Minister of Militia and his deputy and the officers connected with his department should have absolute control of matters of this kind.

My hon. fried (Mr. Ingram) will not persist, I think, in that statement in regard to our giving up entirely the utilization of imperial officers, as the scheme is amplified. I have already referred to the fact that under the British system, which we are adopting, a most important officer, perhaps the most important officer, is the Inspector General. Probably it would be considered wise and desirable that an Imperial officer should be chosen for this position. A most important position will be that of Chief of the General Staff. It might be considered desirable that an imperial officer, for a time, at. least, should occupy that important position. All we want is to have the greatest efficiency possible ; we want to get the best men, whether in Canada or in the imperial army. With reference to what my hon. friend said about political interference, he is confounding two things. I agree with him absolutely in what he says as to promotions. and I challenge him to show that any interference of a political character has taken place in the militia with regard to promotions. I do not believe there has been any such interference worth mentioning ; at any rate I am not aware of it. But when the hon. gentleman comes to the consideration of the organization of a new corps, that is an entirely different thing. When you are organizing a corps de novo, from new material-
Why ?

Why ? If the hon. gentleman would allow me to complete what I was saying, perhaps he would have an opportunity of answering later on.
I say it is an entirely different thing in the case of an already organized military corps, every man in that corps has his rights, from the corporal up, and no man should be placed over his head without a sufficient reason ; certainly no man should be placed over his head for a political reason. I absolutely approve of that proposition and propose standing by it, but when it comes to

organizing a new corps de novo, from such material as may be found throughout the country, taking absolutely new men and new officers, that is an entirely different proposition. In England, as I stated the other day. the course pursued is that an important political official in each county, in the case of the organization of a new corps of militia or volunteers
Does the minister mean to say that the lord-lieutenant of a county is a party, political officer ?
He is appointed by the government. [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And holds his seat with the government.

He is the man who selects the officers. Why 1 Because he is a prominent man. because he is a well known man, and would my hon. friend (Mr. Ingram) say that he himself, as the member for Elgin, if a new corps were to he organized in his county, should not be consulted.
No.
I do not think he would say that.
Yes, he would.

I do not think there is a man in the House would say that. On the contrary, that has always been the custom in this country. When the militia of this country was organized in 1868 members of parliament in my own county and in every county in Nova Scotia, so far as I know, were utilized to organize the militia at that time, and it was done in this way all through the country. That system has resulted well, no objection has been taken to it as far as I have ever heard.
What I rose to say was that when my friend talks about interference with promotions, he is taking a postion with which we will all agree, but when he talks about its being absolutely improper for a prominent man to assist or to take part in the organizing of a new militia corps, I say he is taking an altogether improper view.

In the first place my hon. friend from East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) did not make such a statement as the hon. minister attributes to him. My hon. friend from Bast Elgin did not say that it was wrong to call in politicians to take an interest in the organization of any militia corps. But what my hon. friend from East Elgin did say was that it was absolutely wrong for any politician to introduce partisan politics into the organization of any corps. I take issue at once with the hon. minister in respect to there being any differ-erence between promotion and the organization of a corps de novo. Why should there be any distinction between the two ? I
shall wait for the hon. minister to give some reason why there should be any distinction between the two. Surely, if a Conservative is worthy of being promoted, a Conservative is worthy of being appointed in the first place. Does the hon. minister propose to lay down the doctrine that when a new corps" is to be organized, none but Liberals need apply ? That would be the case if it happened to be in the district presided over by that very broad-minded politician. the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher). None but Liberals need apply ! It would not make a bit of difference whether they were fit for the places or not ; the only qualification necessary would be to subscribe to the Liberal creed, the Liberal doctrine. I am very glad to know that at least this government have thrown off the mask and I wish to congratulate them upon it. They have been publicly pretending before the people of this country that there was no such thing as politics in the administration of the militia and today the right hon. Prime Minister admits that it is quite a proper thing and stands by the Order in Council which he has made to that effect. I know from my own experience that ever since these hon. gentlemen obtained power, they have been grossly partisan in the administration of the militia.
I want to sav to my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence that in the letting of contracts for the supplies of the militia camps, because in the town in which I live a militia camp is situated, these contracts have been given In every case to Liberals not because they were the lowest tenderers and given to them in many cases without any tender whatever.
I wish to contradict my hon. friend immediately and promptly. There have been no contracts made without being open to public tender, and in every case they have been let to the lowest tenderer.
Knowing what I am speaking of I do not propose to take the contradiction of the hon. minister or any other person on the subject.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The rule is
I make this statement and the hon. minister must accept it.
Nobody believes it.
I would not want any such character
Order, order ; sit down.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When an hon. member denies a statement it is the duty of the member making the statement to accept the denial.

If any hon. member makes a statement about a matter which

is absolutely within his own knowledge he is not obliged to accept a contradiction from any other member. Let me tell you that. Mr. Chairman, and I am not the kind of man to take back wator.
I would ask the hon. gentleman to give names and dates. [DOT]
I will give names and dates.
Were the contracts for the Ottawa camp given by tender ?
Order, order.
I am asking the question with the permission of the Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is clear there cannot be two members on the floor at once.
I ask the hon. minister whether the contracts for supplying the camp at Ottawa were made by public tender ?
Yes.
Well, I cannot disPute the statement of the hon. minister.
And I will prove it.
Were these tenders to which I refer publicly advertised for '/
Yes.

The manner in which the hon. gentleman lets these contracts by public tender is 'by sending to a number of gentleman a list. I can tell the hon. minister of a ease where a certain work was to be done, where a certain building was to be erected

But the hon. gentleman is talking about militia camps. The hon. gentleman has made the statement that contracts for supplies for militia camps have been given to political friends without tender and without advertisement. I contradict that absolutely and I demand the names and dates.
Well, I will give both names and dates. I say that they have been given to political friends notwithstanding that others submitted lower tenders.
I say that is untrue.
Very well, I will prove it; that ought to be sufficient.
Give us the names and dates.
I will give the names and dates.
Now.

Do not worry ; I will just choose my own time. I am glad my hon. friend is so amused. I will give the names and dates but I will choose my own time. I say that this thing is being done not only in regard to supplies for the camps but that buildings are being erected by the hon. minister-
The Department of Public Works do that.
This is not a case of the Department of Public Works. This is only a small matter involving a couple of hundred dollars. These are small things.
So are you.

I am just about as big as any one on the other side of the House, and I want hon. gentlemen opposite to understand that I can maintain my position as wTell as they can either in the Horse or out of it. Do not make any mistake about that. I propose to take that position.

The only case I can remember where a building was constructed at a camp without tender was the case of the Lieutenant-Colonel of the 8th Hussars. Lieutenant-Colonel Campbell, a political supporter of the hon. gentleman, constructed stables at Sussex, and the Department of Militia and Defence paid for the building. That is the only case I can recall.

It is not a usual thing for the Department of Militia and Defence to pay for stables constructed by the 8th Hussars. They have always had to pay for them themselves. I am glad that the hon. gentleman has made a new departure in that respect. In this case the tender was not sent to a builder but to a grocer and this occurred in the city of St. John. This gentleman was asked to put in a tender ? I will get the name and give it to the hon. minister.
Very well.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Carried.

No, it is not carried yet.
I want to have a little better explanation than I have had so far from the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence as to what he states about the militia being free from partisan influence. I do not know wThether what he says is true or not. He simply made the statement and we can judge of that statement for ourselves. But, we will take an instance that has created a commotion in this country recently and that is the one which has occurred in the eastern townships. Is it not a fact that the department instructed their officers to reorganize a battalion down there and that the officers carried out their instructions by recommending certain parties to the department ? During all that time, according to the state-

ment made by the bon. Minister of Agriculture, he was writing to citizens asking them to accept certain positions and he tkught he was doing his duty by endeavouring to get them to accept these positions. Was it on account of their military knowledge ? I will not say that it was on account of their partisanship. I do not want to mix party feelings with this question. That is not the question before us. But what I want to point out is that neither the hon. Minister of Agriculture nor any other member of this House who is not delegated with the authority to do so should interfere in a matter in which he has no right to interfere. The persons who were delegated to. reorganize that battalion made certain selections and they reported their selection to the district officer commanding. By him these selections were recommended to the department. That was perfectly proper. It is in the interests of the militia of this country that these selections shall be made without regard to the politics of those who are selected. I care not what their politics are. 1 care not whether they are Conservatives or Reformers.
If your officers are incompetent and are partisans, and will tolerate partisan Tories or Grits solely because they are partisans, then remove your officers. But if your officers are doing what they believe to be in the interests of the Militia, then no member of this House and no minister outside the Minister of Militia has a right to change the names of officers on the list, on account of politics. If we are to understand that members of parliament and ministers of the Crowm have the right to do these things, then I differ from the Minister of Militia and I say that ' under such circumstances you are bound to have a partisan militia and you cannot help it. How on earth can you prevent it, if the foundation of the militia force is based on party lines ? We had the reorganization of a militia battalion in my own city, and I can say that during the time I had the patronage of that county I never interfered in militia matter no more than the man in Halifax. I have always held that it was the duty of the officers to select fit men for the battalions, and if the department is not satisfied, then they should remove the officers. I am zealous" for the success of the battalion in my city, and I am zealous for the welfare of our militia force generally, trusting that they 'will be a credit to Canada, but you can never have that result if you introduce partisanship. I thought the Minister of Militia was," notwithstanding all that had occurred, still in favour of a nonpartisan force, but the statement made by him this morning leaves room for little hope.

I can say, in endorsation of the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram), that in my capacity as a member of parliament I have never in the most remote way interferd w'ith
the militia in my county, because I know my place better than to do anything of the kind. I also endorse the words uttered by the leader of the opposition the other day when he said that politics in connection with the militia was unknown in the province of Nova Scotia. The District Officer Commanding commanding in that province is a prominent Conservative, but I never knew that he allowed his politics to interfere with his duties as commanding the militia in Nova Scotia. Only the other day, I saw that a young officer in the city of Halifax, a young gentleman with whom I am intimately acquainted and who is a prominent Conservative, was promoted. Militia officers should be kept in their positions and promoted, because of their qualifications alone, and if in their positions they begin to interfere with politics, then it is the duty of the government to take notice of it. But, in the formation of a new regiment, the question is not whether a man is a Liberal or Conservative, but w'hether he is the best and the most efficient man in that district to organize that regiment.
Sir' FREDERICK BORDEN. Hear, hear.

I should be very sorry to think, and I should regret it very much if there were the least indication that politics would be introduced into the militia. I think my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Ivaulbaeh), who knows more about the militia of late years than I do, will say that it is his experience when he w'as in command of the battalion in his own county, that there were no politics in the militia.

I heard the Minister of Militia say 'Hear, hear,' when the hon. member (Mr. Ross) gave utterance to sentiments with which we agree on this side of the House, but which were utterly divergent from the sentiments uttered by the minister, wffio said that the case of the formation of a new regiment was entirely different from the question of promotions. The hon. member (Mr. Ross) laid down the same rule both for promotions and for the formation of a new regiment. It is singular that the Minister of Militia cannot understand the plain English used by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Ross) who said, that politics should not be introduced into the formation of a new regiment, and that the only question wffiich should arise was that of the military qualifications of the men appointed as officers. The Minister of Militia said it was entirely different in the case of a new regiment, but he failed to give any reason except that old woman's reason : ' Because.' Well, we all understand what ' because ' means.

I may say that when the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Ross w'as Minister of Militia in the Mackenzie government, there was an attempt made to bring influence on Hon. Alexander Mackenzie to introduce politics into the

formation of a certain regiment, and Alexander Mackenzie's answer was that there must be no political' interference with the militia. I am sorry that rule has' not been rigidly adhered to. I believe that my hon. friend (Mr. Ross) when he was Minister of Militia took the ground that there was to be no political interference, and the same rule was laid down by Sir John Macdonald. As it is now one o'clock and there are a number of gentlemen wlio wish to speak on this question, I think the committee should rise.
At one o'clock, committee took recess.
House recumed at Three o'clock.

I understand that before the recess some remarks were being made with regard to political interference with the militia. I understand that the hon. minister made the statement that when a new regiment was being formed political interference was considered legitimate.
I made no such statement.	.

Then I was misinformed, and I understand that the hon. minister considers that there should not be political interference at any time with regard to the militia. I am very glad indeed to hear him make that statement, because I think it is a course which if pursued will be acceptable to the people of this country, more especially to the militia. But I would like to bring to the hon. minister's notice the fact that'that has not been the case in the past. In my own town, when work has been put up to tender, it has been put up only among those people who are on the patronage list. Now. I hold in my hand a patronage list of the Department of Militia and Defence for the city of St. John, for the year 1902, and I will read it : T. McAvity & Sons, hardware : A. B. McLean, paints, oils, &c.; C. McDonald, paints, oils, &c.; Mooney & Sons, mason ; Win. Melliday, carpenter ; Haley Bros. & Co., carpenter ; G. S. Fisher & Sons, roofing ; John Johnston, painter ; Driscoll Bros., lumber ; P. Campbell & Co., plumber; Jas. Boyle, tinsmith ; C. P. Clarke, drugs ; Canadian Drug Co., drugs ; R. B. Travis, drugs ; R. Leonard, sailmaker ; Godsoe Bros., washing ; O'Brien & Co., stationery ; A. W. Adams, rope ; C. E. Harding & Son, small lumber; A. W. Andrews, repairs, tents, &c.: King & Noble, wood and wood work ; I. E. Smith, wood work and gun platforms ; J. & A. McMillan, stationer. I would like to call the attention of the House to the fact that I. E. Smith, who is put down here for wood work and gun platforms, is a retail grocer in the city of St. John, and not a carpenter at all. I know him very well ; he was for some years an alderman of the city. He obtained the contract for doing 'repairs on the drill shed on the west side of the city of St. John.

Might I make a suggestion to my hon. friend ? I really do not see what bearing this has on the Militia Bill. All my estimates are yet to go through, and my hon. friend will have all the opportunity he wants to discuss this matter. It seems to me that we might now deal with the Militia Bill.
My remarks will not be prolonged, and I will not inflict very much pain on the hon. minister.
I do not mind hearing it, but I think it is out of place, that is all.

The amount of this contract to which I refer W'as a small one, amounting to only $185. But the point I wish to bring out is this, that this work was not put up for tender in the ordinary way, but was put up just among a certain few, and there is no doubt that was done by authority. The officer commanding the district sent down an order to the commanding officer of the regiment to call for tenders among those who were on the patronage list. The list was sent down, and that was done. If that is not bringing polities into the militia, I for one cannot understand what is meant by the term. I might refer to another case. All of us in this House know the gallant colonel who represents the city and county of St. John. At one time he commanded the 62nd regiment in that city, and at the close of his services there was a request from the regiment that he be made honorary colonel of that corps. That was done. I have no objection to that. I do not think any of us have, but shortly after the officer commanding the 3rd. Regiment of Canadian Artillery completed his team of service, and the officers and members of his corps applied to have Lieutenant-Colonel J. R. Armstrong made an honorary colonel of his corps on retirement ; but it was not done. If the hon. minister has any reason that he could give to this House for not considering that request favourably, other than the political reason, I would like to hear it. I may say that Colonel J. R. Armstrong is a Conservative, and a man well known in military matters. He commanded the Shoe-buryness team, aud I think that was the only time that team brought back anything in the shape of rewards. More than that, he has a son who was so imbued with loyal feelings towards this Dominion and the empire, that after making application for a commission in one of the corps that went to South Africa, and finding that he could not obtain one, he resigned his rank and enlisted as a private trooper, and went to serve in the mounted corps. Fortunately he did not lose his life, but was invalided and lost a limb. This gentleman was well thought of in our town. The corps which Col. Armstrong commanded were very much in favour of his being appointed hono-

rary colonel when he retired from the command, and they were very much disappointed when that was not done. If these things do not show a tendency to run the militia on political lines, I would be very glad indeed to hear from the hou. minister that there was some 'other reason for not acceding to the request that was made.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: At this stage 1 would appeal to the committee, in order that we may make some progress, to confine themselves to the clause under discussion.

This clause is very germane to the question at issue. I will just read the clause :
There shall be a Minister of Militia, who shall be charged with and be responsible for the administration of militia affairs.
Now, we want to know whether the Minister of Militia is going to continue in charge of that department or whether some subordinate person is to come in. The minister has said that there is no difference whatever, in regard to the introduction of politics, between the formation of a new corps and promotion in an old corps. I am certain the House misunderstood the minister this morning.

What 1 said was this, that there was a great difference between a corps already established and the composition of a new corps. I said nothing about the introduction of politics into anything. I said that in the case of a corps already existing, every man in it, from the corporal up, had certain rights which must be respected-rights of promotion, if his behaviour was good ; but in the case of a corps not yet in existence, but to be organized, the conditions were entirely different. Selections had to be made. I see no reason why the best and most influential people-and you have to take these people from both sides of politics-should not be consulted to assist in getting the best men to join it.
Then the hon. minister condemns the recent interference of the Minister of Agriculture ?
1 did not say that.
We may take it for granted that he does, as he says he will not allow any more meddling on the part of that Inferior individual in the affairs of the militia.
Order.
HUGHEiS.- Relatively inferior.

I have heard the Minister of Militia say to-day on two occasions that after a regiment has been organized promotion shall be made regularly from one
rank to another. The commander in chief of the land and naval militia, and of all naval and military forces, of and in Canada, is hereby declared to continue and be vested in the Queen.

9. The executive government and authority of and over Canada is hereby declared to continue and be vested in the Queen.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The constitutional principle which governs the raising and control of the militia is of course the same in this country as it is in England. There cau be no departure with respect to His Majesty's forces in this country from the principle that obtains in England. The principle in England I will state briefly from the books, is that the sovereign has not constitutionally any power to raise a military force without the consent of parliament but when a force is raised with that consent, he can, subject to any 'enactment, regulate it in any manner that appears good. Parliament controls the levying of the force, its equipment, maintenance, distribution, payment and all that ; but the control of the force when raised is in the sovereign as head of the executive. The same constitutional rule applies to the colony ; but in the case of the colonial forces, the consent is given by the colonial legislature instead of by the imperial parliament ; so that our position in that respect is the same as that of the imperial parliament. My view with respect to the old Bill, with all due deference to the draughtsman, is that there was an oversight. Some one drew that Bill who had not a proper regard for the true constitutional doctrine that controls the militia. The section in the old Bill reads :
The command in chief of the land and naval militia, and of all military andi naval forces, of and in Canada, is vested in the Queen,

and shall be exercised and administered by Her Majesty personally or by the Governor General as her representative.
It is quite apparent that that section was merely intended to be declaratory of the law ; because we had no power to depart
from the constitutional principle laid down in section 15 of the British North America Act. Therefore a proper form to have adopted would have been : ' The command in chief shall continue to be vested ; ' because we had no power to vest anything in the sovereign, and the doctrine laid down in section 15 of the British North America Act is the old law established after the restoration in a statute of Charles the Second, that tlie control* of the army is vested in the King. That is my first criticism of that section. My next critism is as to the words added. My hon. friend and I differ in this respect. I hold that no word should be put into a statute that can be avoided. If you can avoid the use of unnecessary words, you will confer a blessing on humanity. Words are intended, as a Frenchman once said, to conceal our thoughts rather than to make them clear, which my experience has proved to be true. In this section, after the words,
' vested in the Queen,' where it ought to stop, it says. ' and shall be exercised and administered by Her Majesty personally.' The use of these words is a constitutional heresy. Her Majesty or His Majesty personally has no control oveT the army.
Mr, GOUIU.EY. But in reading the words one would subordinate them to their constitutionality.

stated that the Colonial Defence Committee and the naval authorities in England strongly urged that any work in the direction of organizing a naval militia in Canada should be placed under the control of the Marine and Fisheries Department, because there is already there the nucleus, in a small way, of course, of a naval militia.

The Minister of Marine refused to state to the House the policy of the government on this important question, and now that the naval force is to be taken out of the control of the Minister of Militia, to whom are we to look for information ? In the estimates the government has asked for a vote of $7,500 for this naval force. Is that all the government proposes to do in regard to it ? Let us have some understanding as to what the policy of the government is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There would have
to be somebody.

speechtext:
