Motion agreed to.
Why do you exempt professors of colleges ?
Because we do not think it wise to interrupt the education of the young, and in this we are following the old Act.
I do not see why the professors or teachers should be exempt any more than the business men.
They can volunteer.
But they should be under as much compulsion as any other.
It is not desirable to break up a public institution. Such an institution is different from the store or office of a business man.
It is certainly a great hardship to have a man's business destroyed, quite as great as to have a man taken from his^ position as teacher.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But the hardship in the case of the teacher or professor would be not to the man himself, but to the pupils.

But it is not an injury that cannot be remedied. It only means an interruption, whereas the drafting of a business man means the destruction of his business. It seems to me, that the argument is all the other way so far as the teachers are concerned.
It would mean [DOT] that in the case of a lev6e en masse, the pupils will be taken and the teachers will be left.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen will see, by referring to section 14, that there are two things involved. The section provides first, that all the male inhabitants of Canada of the age of eighteen years and upwards and under sixty, and not exempt or disqualified shall be liable to serve in the militia. That is one thing. But it also provides that the Governor General
may require all male inhabitants of Canada, capable of bearing arms, to serve in the case of a lev&e en masse. In this latter case there is no exemption.
In the case of a levge en masse, would you call out the clergy ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Section 21 of the .Act provides that certain persons shall be exempt from enrolment and from active service, and among these are the clergy. But under section 14 of this Bill in the case of a levee en masse there is no exemption.
What is meant by a levee en massse ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It means that all the inhabitants able to bear arms must go to the front.
Who is to take care of the women and children ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is a matter at the discretion of the executive. Perhaps the women and children might be brought along with the others.

I want to move an amendment to section 15. As at present drafted, members of the Senate, and House of Commons, are exempted from service in the militia. I cannot imagine why this body which ought to set an example to the country, should desire exemption. I would take it as an insult to have such words appear in the statute. I would be in a very bad position in my counti'y, to ask other people to rise and defend the country, if I were exempt myself.
While the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gourley) is exempt, there is nothing to prevent his volunteering.

No, this is invidious, very invidious. The members of the House of Commons should be like others under the law. Then, they will be able to go into the country, and exercise their influence, under proper conditions. It would be a most amazing thing, if the very leaders and directors of public opinion in Canada should be sulking while they asked the ordinary citizen to take up arms in the defence of the country. I regard this as a stigma. Why should we, sitting here as legislators, skulk behind a provision of the law ? We ought to make our position clear, and, I think the judges, who are also exempt under this section, should unite in protest against it. Why should a judge be exempt ? In the case of a conscription,, the judiciary would not be very much affected-only three or four of them would be chosen in the whole of Canada. The wheels of justice would be but little interfered with by such a conscription, and, so far as the House of Commons in concerned, it would mean that only ten or fifteen of our members would be called. And, in order to

ovoid that, it is proposed that we should adopt this section, which would be not in accord with the highest feelings of the people. This is a serious matter. It seems to affect the morale of the country, that the Senate and the House of Commons having the power of legislation should exempt themselves. I really feel like calling upon the self-respect and dignity of the House to eliminate this section. I leave the Senate to look after their own diguity, but I would move that the section be amended so as to remove this exemption of the House of Commons. I find that this exemption is not in the old Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think it is.
I have the old Act here and I cannot find it. The people of the time when this old Act was passed would not stultify themselves so far as to provide for such an exemption.
I think we had better strike it out. It was not in the old Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Was it not ?
No. Strike it out.

If my hon. friend (Mr. Gourley) wants to make the thing complete and be sure that there will be no possible exemption of the House of Commons, I would suggest to him to strike out from the fifteenth line the words * persons disabled by bodily or mental infirmity.'
I do not pretend to be very strong mentally. I am only here as an honest citizen.
I would like to know whether I understood the Minister of Justice correctly. Does he hold that as it stands now there are no exemptions in case of a * levee en masse ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
It seems to me that is hardly a proper way to have it. The country needs people to serve it in all branches.
The Minister of Militia regulates that when he calls out the levee.
Even if that is done 1 can hardly see that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley) is a good one.

I think my hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) is right there. Of course I do not want to throw cold water on the patriotism of anybody, but we must have some common sense besides patriotism. Suppose that in the case of a levee eti masse we keep no person to look after the jails.
In that case the prisoners would go to the front too.
But at the same time what will you do with the wardens and officers of lunatic asylumns ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That will be the responsibility of the executive.

We must have common sense in these things. If the minister tells us that the Governor General may make some exemptions in a levee en masse all right, but if the law is to read as it is now according to clause 14, the Governor General cannot make any exemptions and every one in the country may be called out. It may create an awkward position.

If every one was called only a few would be selected. The Gospel says that 1 many are called but few are chosen.' The Governor General in Council under this law has the right to call every one, but in the administration of that right the department would make such exceptions as might be necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In case of national emergency you cannot have any exceptions; you have to trust to the good sense of the administration of the day.
I would like to know, not by the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley), if the Governor General in Council or the Governor General will have any right to discriminate in case of a levee en masse.
It is done by a military officer not by the Governor General. In that connection
Iam not speaking to myt hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes). If he will excuse me I have the floor and I am putting a question politely to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick).

I am going to ask a question, and I do not think that the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), with all his nerve, has the right to say when 1 shall or shall not speak. If he will be good enough to look after the disruptive elements of the empire it will keep him busy. Under the amendments no member of parliament can claim exemption. It should be clear that any militia man who is a member of this House should be free to use what language he chooses in conformity with the institutions of this House and of this country, and that no enactment here should possibly bring him under the control of any militia force which would prevent us having a free parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My answer t0 the last difficult conundrum propounded by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes) is that there is no exemption in

favour of a member of parliament. He would be obliged, with every one else, when called upon, to take service, but a summons to parliament would supersede the call to arms and he would be entitled to answer his summons to parliament. I am not familiar with the subject of the lev6e en masse, except in so far as my general reading applies, and I take it that a levee en masse refers to cases of national peril, national danger, when the people of the country capable of bearing arms must go to the assistance of the country.	Of course it would be a matter for the exercise of discretion to see to it that the national peril was not increased by allowing the lunatics and criminals to escape, and leaving the women and children unprovided for. That would be adding to the national burden and it will be assumed that those in charge will see that all these interests are provided for.
This same amendment should be made to apply to the provincial legislatures.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think that if one goes out the other should go out.
Provincial legislators go out.
Do I understand that the amendment of the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley) is accepted ?
Yes.
I do not think it is proper. It is simply giving way
Oh, oh.

Well, if the time should come when it would be necessary for any one to go to the front, I think I would be there before many people who talk war all the time in this House. But I think it is perfectly ridiculous to give way to an appeal to prejudice of that kind. I think it is necessary for parliament to keep itself going, just as necessary as the other public services, and therefore, if we are prepared to exempt the judges, the deputy ministers, the professors of colleges and universities, it would be just as proper to keep the members of parliament, both federal and provincial, in the list of exemptions. I think it is giving way to a small appeal to militarism which is not going to appeal to many sensible people outside of this House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Sir Frederick Borden moves to insert the following subclause :
Members of the naval -militia, members of the police force and fire brigade in incorporated cities, towns and villages-
In many cases ' fire brigade ' would cover the whole male population.
I think not.
Oh, yes.
I know that in my own town practically the whole male population belongs to the fire brigade. I think it is true of every small town.
We might say * cities.'

Very well, that was the idea I had.
Firemen permanently employed in incorporated cities, towns and villages.
By the police force I meant the officers and men permanently employed in the police force.
If you take every man away what is the use of leaving the police force at home ?

I object to the amendment proposed. That proposed by the minister was ail right, that the police forces and fire brigades should be exempted. If you make it read in that way it will give exemption only to the fire brigades and police forces of the large towns and cities where policemen and firemen are employed all the year round, and you will place policemen and firemen in the smaller villages In an awkward position. They have very small fire 'brigades and only three or four policemen in these small villages, and they have to do something else to earn their living. If you force them into the militia you impose a hardship upon them. I do not see why you should pass legislation for the large cities and not for the small villages. T understood that an amendment was proposed to cover, not only the large cities, but the small villages as well, but you strike out the small villages and towns from the benefit of that provision. I know that in my own province in many places the fire brigades and police forces are not permanently employed. They are supposed to give their services alternately. They have fire brigades in several of the towns and villages in Quebec in which one man will give his services for so many days in the month. They organize voluntary fire brigades of eight or ten men, who look after the safety of the village from fire, and at the same time earn their living.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is proposed to amend the clause by adding the following paragraph :
Members of the naval militia and members of police force and fire brigade permanently employed in incorporated cities, towns and villages.

The hon. minister may remember that I gave him notice of a



proposed amendment, that people who have religious objections to taking up arms shall be required to furnish a substitute or bear any expense in providing the substitute incurred by the government. I do not believe in interfering with peoples' religious doctrines or forcing them to fight, but I think that any person who enjoys the protection of the government and of the militia should be required to provide a substitute.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This is simply a re-enactment of the law as we have it. Paragraph 3 provides that persons of different forms of religious belief-
Shall be exempt from such service when balloted in time of peace or war, upon such conditions and under such regulations as the Governor in Council from, time - to time prescribes.
Then you can make regulations to cover the case of a substitute.
The exemption shall be provided for by regulation.

What is the necessity for putting this in at all ? I do not see why you should publish it to the world that people having a certain religious belief may come here and be exempt. I think it is sufficient to deal with the emergency when it arises. We have thousands of people in Manitoba who will not take up arms, and I think this provision could be left out and the matter dealt with when the emergency arises.

They came into the country knowing that this provision was in our militia law, and I think it is only fair that we should continue the provision, which is to 'be under the control and subject to regulations to be .issued by the Governor General in Council.
Apart from that, I understand that the Mennonites came in some years ago with the understanding that they "would not be asked to take up arms.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under the Militia Act every person bearing a certificate from the Society of Quakers, Mennonites or Tunkers, is exempt under such conditions and under such regulations as the Governor in Council prescribes.
If you will look at section 2, you will see that ' prescribed ', means prescribed by this Act or by regulations.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Well, then, you need not amend that ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is all right.
What I want to impress upon the hon. minister is that in his regulations provision shall be made for that point. These regulations, I presume, will be submitted to parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes ; under the law they are obliged to be submitted to parliament.
I hope that point will be covered.
The regulations will be made before the Act goes into force.

Before this clause is carried, I would like to point out to the hon. minister that persons who claim exemption have, under paragraph 3 of section 15, to give their notice at least one month before they claim their exemption, and that by section 16 they have to give proof of the ground upon which they ask exemption. Does that mean that in case of the organization of a corps in any district persons who may be exempted or who may be called are, if they have not filed their exemption one month before, bound to serve for the time for which they are called, and that the exemption will only ajjply when they are called the second time ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The service is not compulsory.

There is a clause in the Bill which allows the Governor in Council to call people up for enrolment in any district of the country in order to fill the ranks when there are not sufficient volunteers. Therefore, it is useless to say enrolment is voluntary. It is voluntary as long as there are people enough willing to engage. Suppose the Governor General in Council decides to organize a regiment in a district of the country in which the people do not come forward to enlist, you have all the powers here necessary to enforce them to come in within their classes. You call the first class, then the second class, then the third class and then the fourth class, and then they are enrolled by ballot. Suppose a man is called by ballot and is enrolled, should he have filed his claim for exemption at least one month before his enrolment ? He has not filed his exemption because nobody thinks of filing this exemption and if he does not desire to serve voluntarily what would be his position ? Will they be. subject to the enrolment, and will their proof be useless if they have not given notice one month before they are called.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think so.

If that is the case, as 1 understand the Minister of Justice to say it is, it would be very hard indeed on certain persons. While the general principle prevails that every citizen is supposed to know the law, yet it" would be rather an extreme view to * take of ' it, that every citizen should know that the clauses of this Bill oblige him to give notice one month before even he may suppose that he may be called. I believe this provision should be stricken out of the Bill.
Or else, there should be a provision that when a man is called upon to be enrolled by ballot, he should have a certain delay to prove exemption.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That "would be covered by section 33 of the Bill which gives the Governor General in Council power to make regulations.
But suppose they do not make regulations. This Bill will provide for one month's notice and you incorporate that in the Act, and do not leave it to regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It may be necessary to enroll the militia at any time without thirty days' notice. There is something to be said on both sides, and I think this matter can be left to the regulations.
We ought to be informed that there is some great pressing necessity for such a clause as this.

This law has been .on the statute-book for forty or fifty years and no hardship has ever resulted from it. The suggestion of the -Minister of Justice is the correct one, namely, that this matter will be dealt with by regulation.	'

Section agreed to.
Section 17 agreed to.
Section 18 stricken out.

Sir FREDERICK BORDEN moved to strike out the words ' cadets or.'
HUGHES, is there any definition of what a cadet corps is.

The reason I ask is that a great many public schools are wishing to form a cadet force corps.

Many young men who enlist for three years' service drop out after one year. It is perfectly useless for a young man to go to camp for only one year. I think the terms of the engagement should be strictly enforced.

I agree with my hon. friend that it is desirable that young men should continue in the service for the full term ; but I do not agree with him that it does not do a young man good to go for only one year.

If you force a young man to go to camp when he perhaps loses a good job for doing so, you will be unable to get another young man from the same neighbourhood to go to camp afterwards. I think the increased pay will have the desired effect.	[DOT]

speechtext: He goes as a matter of course.

Amendment agreed to.
On clause 26-military districts and subdivisions.
Sir FREDERICK BORDEN moved to strike out this clause and insert the following in its stead :
The Governor in Council may direct that any portion of Canada shall be a military district for the purposes of this Act and may cause two or more districts to be grouped together for the purposes of command and administration, and may divide any military district into such sub-districts, brigade, regimental or company divisions as may appear expedient.
Motion agreed to.
On section 27-constitution of active militia.

I beg to move that the following section be inserted between sections 27 and 28 :
That the total peace establishment of the active militia shall not exceed fifty thousand men.
Under the old Act there was no limit. There was no limitation provided. But in the clause providing for the training of men, clause 58, there was .a limitation of the number to 45,000 active militia men. It limited the power of the government to order the training of more than 45,000. This clause is omitted in the present Bill, so that in the Bill which is before us there is no limit whatever to the number of corps that may be organized by the minister, and there is no limitation whatever to the peace or war establishment of the militia, no limitation to the number of men that may be drilled every year. I think it is about time that we should pause a little and reflect on the proposed increase of our militia, and the expenditure connected with it. I admit that we have been passing through a period of military enthusiasm, which has been kept up in this House by a few military gentlemen like the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes), and a few laymen like my hon.
The statute now existing to which my hon. friend refers provides that 40,000 is the minimum number that should be trained ; it is not at all a limitation.
That is what I said. I said there was no limitation at present except as regards the number to be trained.

I understood him to say there was a limitation to the number that could be trained. I have taken the trouble to look up the old debates, and to read a speech made by Sir Geo. Cartier in 1868 in introducing his Bill, which was modified in later years by Sir Adolphe Caron. I And that Sir Geo. Cartier made this remark :
He expected under the provisions of this Bill to provide that the number of trained men within the Dominion should not be less than 40,000.
So he was providing for the compulsory training of 40,000 men. Sir Adolphe Caron, in introducing his amendments in 1883, said:
I have taken the number of men as laid down in the original Bill.
He introduced a provision by which the number of 45,000 might be drilled by authority of Order in Council. Now it seems to me that a limitation of this section is undesirable. I think it is undesirable that any particular number of men should be named in the Bill as necessary to be drilled. That is a matter that should be left to parliament and to the government to regulate from time to time as the government may deem expedient. My hon. friend knows quite as well as I do that no training can be done, no drilling can' be done, without the authority of parliament. That is an expensive operation, that requires money, and each year we have to come to parliament and make a statement of the number of men we propose to train and we ask for money for that purpose. We are absolutely tied up and limited to the amount of money which parliament sees fit to vote us. I think it is undesirable that any limitation of this kind should he placed in this Bill. In a clause which will come later, I have placed a limitation to the number of the active militia. The active militia, as my hon. friend has shown, at the present time, is somewhere about
45,000	officers and men, about the number named in the present Bill ; and I propose to give to the Governor in Council power, under a clause which we will come to later on, to call out the whole of the active militia, subject of course, as it always must be, to the vote of parliament.

I am glad to concur in the view taken by the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden). I am glad that there are many subjects on wrhich members of parliament can agree, affecting the genera] interests of the country. I concur in the proposition of the Minister of Militia and will go further. I see that a malicious effort is being made to persuade the people that because we desire to get into a state of preparation for defence we are introducing militarism. I do not know what militarism means ; I cannot give it an intellectual meaning as applied to this country. I know what it means in the old world, but in regard to many countries where they have been overridden by militarism I am bound to say, as a student, that I believe it has proved a benefit. I believe that the great and unprecedented advance that Germany has made in commercial progress in the past twenty-five or thirty years, has been due, in a large measure, to her system of conscription. And I would not be averse, while glorying in freedom, while believing that every man in this country should be free, to the establishment of some measure of conscription. I believe that the German government has given to that nation great power and virility given it great creative power, by taking young men at the age of fourteen, when perhaps they would be idle about the streets and putting them for four years in the army. In that way they are not only given military drill but are given a splendid mechanical education and after they leave the army they are ready to enter factories. Why lias Germany become a great manufacturing country in twenty-five years ? Because these men are trained in the army to habits of industry and discipline and are given a good mechanical training so that when they leave the army they are fit, with very little training, to go into a factory and become producers. If Germany has risen in twenty-five years from a weak commercial state into a powerful commercial state that result is due to militarism.

What about the progress
that has been made by the United States ?

Some hon. gentlemen go about the country thinking evidently that the people of Canada are under-educated and under-bred. I tell the hon. gentlemen opposite that in the county which I have the honour to represent there is not one man who possesses less intelligence than any man in the House of Commons of Cana la, and if I should undertake to indulge in clap-trap of that kind, in talk of militarism I would have a dozen men asking me : What do you mean by mi-

litarism ? I would ask these lion, gentlemen or any hon. gentleman in this House : What (lo you mean by militarism ?

I have no fear that if we get into trouble with any nation, England, Scotland and Ireland, or Scotland, Ireland and England-the latter will perhaps satisfy my hon. friend better- would come to our defence, but only on condition that we help ourselves, and I say that we cannot spend money better than by supplying our young men with rifles and teaching them how to shoot. I say again that I hope the hon. member for Labelle is alone in holding the sentiments he has expressed in this House.

It is only right that we should judge this amendment by its own terms and not by the extravagant meanings that have been ascribed to it. It appears that the member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) has got himself into this position, that if he found it necessary to read the Ten Commandments to this Housei, there are a number of hon. gentlemen here who would get up at once and denounce them as disloyal, traitorous and anti-British. Now, Mr. Chairman, clause 27 that we-have just passed, in its first two lines, plainly gives the Governor General in Council power to organize as many regiments as he pleases. That means that when at any time the public mind Is inflamed, whether in regard to internal or external politics, some Minister of Militia who may be holding that office might take it into his head to organize to a tremendous extent ; and every man knows that when a responsible minister has done a thing and afterwards comes to parliament and asks for its endorsement, the party supporting the governmentt of which he is a minister will not turn him down. We know that in such a case tho House of Commons would sanction an act of which it would have disapproved if it could have voluntarily pronounced upon it in the beginning. Now, the member for Labelle moves an amendment that the peace establishment of the active militia shall be limited to 50,000. At the present time we have not got 50,000 on the peace establishment ; therefore, he is not asking the minister to reduce the number, he is still leaving a margin up to which any ministei may recruit before lie is obliged to come to parliament. If then there is any necessity fof it, parliament can increase the number beyond 50,000. I say, with all due respect to those who have put forward alarmist notions this afternoon, that the amendment of the hon. member for Labelle should only be

considered on its own merits and not in view of the meanings that have been ascribed to it, merely because it comes from a ei rtain source. Now, there is no doubt that the people are getting alarmed at the growth of our militia expenditure. I think we have seen this afternoon that it is almost impossible at the present time for some hon. gentlemen in this House to discuss militia matters in a sane and reasonable manner. It seems to me that an amendment of this kind, and perhaps other amendments limiting the power of the Minister of Militia during the recess of parliament, are right and proper, and should be adopted by this committee.
Amendment (Mr. Bourassa) negatived.
On section 28, with the form of oath as follows :
X	swear that I will well and
truly serve Our Sovereign Lord the King, his
heirs and successors in the	tor
the term of	years or until lawfully
discharged, dismissed or removed, and that I will resist His Majesty's enemies and cause His Majesty's peace to be kept and maintained. and that I will in all matters appertaining to my service faithfully discharge my duty according to law. So help me God.

I propose to strike that form of oath out, and insert the following in lieu thereof :
I, A B,. do solemnly promise and swear (or solemnly declare) that I will he faithful and true, and bear true allegiance to His Majesty.
Mr. FOW'LER. This is a very excellent change, and simplifies the oath. But the minister has left out the term of years in this section.

This is actually the old oath.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 29 :
The permanent force shall consist of such permanently embodied corps, not exceeding two thousand men, as are, from time to time, authorized by the Governor in Council

I propose to strike out that clause and replace it by the following :
The permanent force shall consist of such permanently embodied corps, not exceeding 2,000 men, enrolled for continuous service, as are from time to time authorized by the Governor in Council.
This amendment is found necessary. We have added an Engineer Corps, an Ordinance Corps and an Army Service Corps ; and we are adding to depots, one to be located at Montreal, with probably 200 men, and one somewhere in the Northwest Territories, with probably 100 mounted men. Later on there will be a depot in British Columbia.
Mr. FOWLER, Is there a permanent corps in Nova Scotia ?

No ; but we have a depot and permanent corps in New Brunswick, which answers every purpose. Once a year the artillery is brought to Halifax from the country districts for instruction with the regulars.
Where do the officers get their certificates for training ?
At Fredericton.
Will the permanent corps that is to be organized in the Northwest permit of the Mounted Police being moved further on ?

Yes, there will probably be a small detachment. As the country settles up. the militia will gradually supply the place of the Northwest Mounted Police! and the police will go [DOT] further north to more remote districts.
Mr. FOWLER, These will be mounted ?
It will be a cavalry corps or mounted infantry.
How many constitute a corps for a district ?
That depends on what arm it is. About 100. The mounted infantry is about SS or 89 and the infantry from 100 to 125. There are 100 in a company.
How many are there at London, for instance ?
One hundred.
I think I will ask you to add a couple of hundred more. Two hundred at Truro would be a great education for us.

Two thousand, I think, will supply the number.
Sections 35 to 44 allowed to stand.
On section 45-appointment of district officers.
Sir FREDERICK BORDEN moved that the following be inserted as subsection (a) :
The pay and allowances to officers of the General Staff, Head-Quarters Staff and District Staff, not provided for by this Act, shall be fixed by the Governor in Council.
What is the present salary of the General Officer Commanding ?
Mr. FOWLER, These will not exceed that amount ?

I do not know whether it is worth while bringing it up now but I think a great many officers throughout the country would like to know what the hon. minister's intention is in regard to officers. The pay of the men is fairly satisfactory. If the hon. minister is not ready to give an expression to-night I will not press it.

I cannot to-night but I think before we get through with the estimates I may be able to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 46-commissioned, warranted, and non-commissioned officers.

Why not use the term ' Governor in Council ' instead of ' His Majesty'? It is only a matter of form. The change has been made in all the other clauses of the Bill.
' Sir FREDERICK BORDEN. There has always been some fiction of this kind in reference to His Majesty and we thought we would leave it.
Why not have the reality and say by the Governor in Council ?
The fiction has been left aside and the reality taken up by the hon. minister in sixteen other clauses. I do not see why the fiction should' remain in this clause.
It is sixteen to one.
In clauses 45 and 44 you provide that the appointment shall be made by the Governor in Council.
Since we have done so well, perhaps my hon. friend will allow that to stand.
Why ? If there is a reason given I have no objection but it seems to me we might as well be logical. It is only a matter of form.
HUGHE'S. The hon. gentleman has never seen a commission.
I have seen a commission. I have seen the commission of my grandfather and of my great grandfather granted when they served in the militia.
I am glad the hon. gentleman has ancestors who have served in the militia.
Let this clause stand and I will make inquiries about it.
The commissions are signed by the Governor General.

And signed by the minister also. There is something in Sir F. W. BORDEN.
section 47 about the commission being signed by the Governor General.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The commissions are granted by the Governor General and you canuot change that.

That settles it then.
On section 47-Governor's signature to commissions.

I think this is the same as the old law and although it would have been a very great job to have these all signed I know the officers of the militia would think much more of their commissions if they were all signed.
On section 50-rank of officers in time of peace.
As soon as the brigadier-general is out of office will he go back to the rank of colonel ?

That is only temporary. That is the rule in England. He only takes the rank of Brigadier-General during the time he is in charge of the brigade camp.
On section 51-rank of officers when called out.
Will this be only temporary ?
No, I think not.
The term ' emergency ' has a very broad range.
Section 51 applies to qualified officers. It would not apply to any one who was not a qualified officer.
Suppose there was a riot in Toronto or Montreal and an officer \vas sent down to deal with it. He might dispose of it in a couple of hours and he would be a major general.
We would have to take our chances on that.
Why not confine this to active service in time of war ?

It would be done under regulation anyway.
On section 52-Honorary rank on retirement.

Why confine that to officers of the Headquarters Staff ? We know of some officers who have given their time throughout long and useful lives to the militia force, some in command of districts now whose names occur to me. I do not care to mention any. It seems to me that it should not be made to apply to the headquarters alone.
I have no objection.
I drew the hon. minister's attention to that when it was up before.
Yes; I know.
It also contains the words ' or in the department.' What does that mean ?
In the Militia Department, I suppose.
It provides that the civil servants in the Militia Department are eligible.

Why not leave it at the word ' appointments ' and strike out all the rest except the words 'for valuable services rendered to the country.' I beg to move the words ' on the Headquarters Staff or in the Department ' be struck out.
Would the minister interpret an executive officer to mean the District Officer Commanding ?
No question about it. I move to insert the word ' staff ' instead of the word ' executive.'

I think it is better.
Section as amended agreed to.
Section 53 stricken out.
Section 54 agreed to without discussion.
On section 55,
Officers of His Majesty's regular army serving in Canada may be granted a temporary commission in the militia of rank equivalent to their army rank and antedated to have the same date as that of their imperial commission.
That is a proper thing to do.
We have officers serving here temporarily and I think we should only give them the rank they have as imperial officers.
I am very strongly in favour of that. I do not believe in giving these regular army officers superior rank to our Canadian officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Hear, hear, you are a good Canadian.
I am a good Canadian and a gwd Britisher ; you're right I am.
This will not prevent giving them senior rank if you choose to.

No.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 56-uniform and equipment of officers.
Officers of the militia shall provide their own uniform and equipment, with the exception of mounted corps, to whom saddlery may be issued as prescribed
I move that the word ' officers ' be substituted for the word ' corps.'
Amendment agreed to.
Officers' uniforms are too expensive in this country and the result is that in many cases you cannot get first class men to take commissions.
No doubt.
For instance, it is perfectly absurd to have these Hussar uniforms in this country.
I agree with the hon. gentleman.

The best men to officer cavalry regiments are men brought up on the farm and used	to	riding
horses. You must as a rule draw your rank and file from the country districts. If you officer a regiment from the rural districts with the sons of rich men from the city the result is not Satisfactory. Many of these city officers put on so much side and style that the men do not like them. It is very important that the department should simplify the uniform and render it less expensive.

I agree with the hon. gentleman, and I hope the time will soon come when we will be able to adopt some sensible, simple aud useful uniform, which will be of a Canadian type. I do not know why in the world we should stick to these old uniforms, which of course have a history in England, which they wish to preserve, but which so far as we are concerned are useless importations. I believe we should adopt a system of our own.

I endorse what has been said by the Minister of Militia. I have been to the Laprairie camp recently and it is absurd to see our soldiers exposed to the heat of the sun wearing small caps that did not cover the half of the head. A straw hat would not cost any more and would be much more serviceable. Let us have a good Canadian uniform which will be far better suited to our needs than these imported things from over the sea.
I am in favour of a common sense Canadian uniform which will suit not only in Canada but anywhere in the world.
You need not go out of Canada to And common sense.

The men in charge of the Laprairie camp did not know their

business, because if they had asked they could have had straw hats issued instead of the caps. Our corps have been using straw hats in camp for years.
Or light helmets.

It was neglect on the part of the officers that the men did not have straw hats. I agree with my good friend (Mr. Fowler) with regard to officers' uniforms, and I think the government should meet the cost to a certain extent. In England, volunteer officers get an appropriation in lieu of uniform, and I am satisfied that every officer in Canada would prefer an allowance for uniform to the beggarly pittance he now receives. The minister has today seen the influence which the member for I.abelle (Mr. Bourassa) has in the House, and if he provides a common sense uniform to be supplied to the militia officers, he will be endorsed heartily by the people of Canada.

If the department provides that the officers' uniform shall be simple, useful and economical, the officers would purchase it themselves. It takes from $800 to $1,000 to fully equip an hussar officer with uniform and accoutrements, and that is perfectly absurd.
I think so.

I c'o not know whether my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) knows anything about militia matters now or not, but we have it on the authority of the great minister of war who meddled in the eastern townships regiment, that the cost of a uniform, is $55, sword and all. I do not think an officer should be called upon to expend even $55 on his uniform. It is true, some officers in those swell corps go to an expenditure that is quite uncalled for. There is no regulation in force in Canada that requires any officer in a city or other corps to purchase an expensive uniform. That was settled in the House in favour of the less expensive uniform ; so that no man now need get an expensive uniform unless he wants to become a dandy, and I think there are few of the officers foolish enough for that.

I have seen my hon. friend from North Victoria dressed out in full uniform, and will guarantee that it costs more than $55, and no man would wish to appear shabby in a regiment beside my hon. friend from Victoria. The cost of tile uniform should be the same for all officers, so that there would not be any possibilily of a man going beyond his means in order to provide himse f with as good a uniform as that of 'his neighbour.

Hate any complaints come from soldiers who have purchased their uniforms, and have had to wait for Mr. SAM. HUGHES.
months to get their money from the department ?
I have not heard of any.

Take the staff sergeants, for instance. The government allows them $44, or something like that, for their clothing, and it costs them about $60, and I think they have had to wait for some time to get their money. Have there not been complaints of that kind ?
Sir FREDERIC^ BORDEN. I have not heard of any, but I will inquire.
On section 57-importation of saddlery free of duty.
Is it not a new departure to supply saddles to the militia ?
Yes.
Will the minister give us an idea what it costs for saddlery ?
About $40, I think:
Do the men get the same as the officers ?
I think they do.
Who inspects the saddles ?

If my hon. friend will wait until we come to the estimates, I shall be very glad to give him all the information. It is a mcst extraordinary thing to mix militia stores up with the Militia Bill. The inspector of saddlery in this city is Lieutenant-Colonel Brown.
Is he a practical saddler ?

I believe he is. At any rate, he is the commanding officer of the cavalry corps here. He has done the work for a long time, and done it satisfactorily. He did it for the imperial government for a year or two, while saddles were being shipped to the old country, and I believe he gave entire satisfaction. The inspector in Toronto is an old English sergeant of the name of Woodcock. Lieutenant-Colonel Graveiey is in charge of the stores there. These are all I can remember at the present moment.
Section 57-Importation free of duty- struck out.
On section 58-responsibility for damages-

With regard to deficiency in equipment, I do not care how careful an officer commanding a regiment or company may be, there are bound to be some shortages, some lcsses,,in every camp of instruction, after the articles have been
<5461

in use for a few years ; and it has struck me as a hardship-and it has impressed the men in the force in the same way-that after some article has been in use for four of five years, and is perhaps more than half worn out,' it should be charged up against the commanding officer at its first cost price. It seems to me some regulation might be made by which a certain reasonable life would be assigned to every article. For instance, in the old days it would be easy to ascertain the life of a haversack or a knapsack, and write off each year a certain amount ; so that when an article was lost, the officer would be charged with its value at the time of the loss. When the new rifles were given out in place of the old Sniders, some of the old rifles were lost, and the proposition was to charge them up at $25 each, the original cost of the rifle, when at that very time the same rifle was selling at Eaton's and Simpson's in Toronto as a curiosity at $1 and $1.25 each. I call the attention of the minister to this in the hope that something will be done in making a regulation along the line I have indicated.
On the first draft of the Bill I drew the minister's attention to this very thing, and he promised to attend to it in the regulations.
That is in the hands of the officers now.

Section agreed to.
Section 59 agreed to.
On section 60-when only men may appear in uniform
This is an old law.

Some of the soldiers object to being compelled to wear uniform, when others are allowed to go in civilian clothing. I have a complaint on that subject which it may be worth while to read :
Formerly non-commissioned officers and men as above were occasionally allowed the privilege when on leave of wearing plain clothes, and it was much appreciated by those who had the good fortune to obtain such leave. Now, however, fall is changed and militia order 225 (4J of 1903 was issued cancelling such privileges. Now, Sir, a recruit of about three months' service can get an employed job as a servant to an officer, do his chores, and blacken his boots, and empty the slops, result, he can walk out in plain clothes because he is an officer's servant. Also, he does no duty, does no guard or fatigues, just merely attends to his master alone. Is he of high born degree that such a most unfair regulation should be made in his case as allowing him to wear plain clothes ? The cook in the officer's mess and the assistant cook, grooms, and the pantry waiters in the officer's mess are all privileged to wear plain clothes when off duty to walk out in^ but a well conducted soldier, or a non-commissioned 206
officer of over fifteen years' service are refused this privilege. Why ?
Officers as a general rule only wear their uniform about four hours a day when one can run across them down town in ' mufti ' almost daily. Why should not non-commissioned officers be allowed it ? Policemen are, postmen are, asylum employees are, jail-keepers are, but Tommy Atkins of the permanent force is the worst of all, and he, poor fellow, must wear the uniform night and day. To add to the discomfort1 the hottest days in summer he must tramp to church in a heavy cloth tunic flannel-lined, heavy leather waist belt tightly fastened around waist (if it is a. little loose, you are reprimanded on paro'le for slovenliness) and a big helmet and everything imaginable to add to the discomfort of a soldier in July and August,
It is not necessary that I should go or. with a lot of this stuff.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not at all necessary

But if there are such privileges granted, they should be open to every well-conducted soldier. No one will pretend that on a day like this, a lined tunic, a big heavy helmet and a belt tied tightly around the waist, would add to a man's comfort.
I am not aware of the circumstances, but will make inquiry.
This clause only covers the ordinary active militia, and not the permanent corps.

I suppose regulations will be made to cover the cases of the permanent corps.
On section 63-annual drill.

I move that the clause be amended so that it will read as follows :
The Governor in Council may order the active militia, or any portion thereof, to drill or train for a period of not more than thirty days in each year.
Why do you strike out the minimum ?
We might want to drill a certain corps for only four or five days, and we do not want to be tied up.

Motion agreed to.
On section 64,
Officers, warrant officers and non-commissioned officers of the permanent force shall be entitled to daily pay and allowances at rates to be prescribed.
2. The Governor in Council may, from time to time, fix the sums to be paid to privates of the permanent force, regard being had to length of service, good conduct and efficiency ; but the ordinary pay shall not exceed the amounts following, that is to say :-

Cents.
For privates per diem	75
For buglers under 18 years of age, per diem	40
Is the pay of a private increased from 40 cents a day ?
It will begin now at 50 cents and increase according to length of service and good conduct to 75 cents.
You intend to increase the minimum figure under this clause ?
Yes.

What is the meaning of the word ' ordinary pay ' ?
. Sir FREDERICK BORDEN. That is inserted because special corps, labourers, &c., are given special pay, not the ordinary pay.
Are they not sworn in as members of the permanent corps V
They are.
Would 'permanent corps ' not be the correct words to use here ? A man in the stores department gets $1.25 a day, but he wears his uniform and is sworn in. Is he not a member of the permanent force ?
He is not in barracks.
Where does the minister get authority to pay a man in the stores department $1.25 a day ?
He gets it from a special vote for pay and allowances.
Would not this clause keep him from getting it 1
I think that would be a matter of regulation.

You cannot override an Act of parliament by a regulation. If the law says you shall not pay him more than 75 cents a day there may be difficulty in paying the man $1.25. I am only pointing it out for the safety of the men.
I think the interpretation was that the expression * ordinary pay ' overcame that difficulty.
Is it the intention to increase also the pay of the officers, warrant officers, and non-commissioned officers as well as of the privates ?
My hon. friend (Mr. Gilmour) will see that the pay of non-commissioned officers is based upon that of the privates ; it is so much more than that of the privates.
How much V

A sergeant-major gets $1.50, a warrant officer gets $1.25 and $1, but there will be an increase.
On section 65-pay of active militia.

I have an amendment to be substituted for section 65b. It was arranged in the Committee of the Whole some time ago. It is as follows :
For privates at the rate of 50 cents a day, which rate may be increased as may be prescribed, but not to exceed a maximum of $1 a day.
I have also an addition to be inserted as section 65c which is as follows :
An allowance of $1 per diem or such other rate as is prescribed shall be paid to each officer and man for every horse necessarily used by him on active service, during the period of active drill, or when otherwise on duty as aforesaid.
We omitted in the Bill to make any provision to pay for horses. This simply is restoring the clause which is in the present law.
This is not intended as a slap at the new war lord for hiring his horse ?

You must riot be so vindictive.
Section as amended agreed to.
Progress reported.
